Confusing the two strips protection from babies, people with profound cognitive disabilities and anyone unable to reciprocate. And even those who accept the premise don't reach the conclusion: lacking rights, in the strict legal sense, doesn't authorize causing suffering.
"Animals have no duties, don't pay taxes, don't obey any law. So they can't have rights."
The classic formulation is Carl Cohen's, in a 1986 article in the
defending the use of animals in research:
Rights arise, and can only be defended, among beings who make, or can make, moral claims on one another.
Animals lack the capacity to understand and apply moral rules.
So animals have no rights, and in Cohen's words, "they can have none".
Those without rights may be used, subject to any duties of kindness.

Cohen anticipates the objection from humans lacking this capacity and replies that the capacity for moral judgment "is not a test to be administered to human beings one by one", because "the issue is one of kind". That way out is examined in chapter A11.

The same structure appears in contractualism: morality would be an agreement among rational agents, and only parties to the agreement would be protected by it. It's worth noting that John Rawls, although he excluded animals from the domain of justice, held that we have duties of compassion and humanity toward them.
fails at P1, which confuses who makes rules with whom the rules protect, at P2, which is partly false, and at P3, which doesn't follow: lacking legal rights isn't the same as moral permission.
"When the cow signs the constitution, we'll talk."
"Are you going to prosecute a shark for murder?"
"Rights exist only among beings able to make moral claims on one another." (Cohen)
"Morality is an agreement among those who can understand and follow rules."
"They aren't part of our moral community."

A newborn baby doesn't know what a rule is, doesn't help anyone and doesn't return favors. Even so, everyone agrees no one may hurt a baby. That shows something important: being protected isn't a prize you earn by fulfilling obligations. It's what is owed to those who can be hurt. Animals work the same way.
The argument swaps two different things.
are those who can have duties;

are those who can be harmed. Babies, people with advanced dementia and people in a coma are patients without being agents, and they don't lose protection for that. Our whole legal system works this way, with guardians representing those who can't claim anything. Besides, even those who deny animals rights, like Carl Cohen, admit we have duties regarding them.
"Does a baby have duties? Then why does it have rights?"
The argument lives on a conceptual confusion that moral philosophy resolved long ago.
Someone who can have duties and be held responsible
Someone who can be harmed or benefited
Babies, people with dementia, people in a coma, animals
Every moral agent is also a patient, but not every patient is an agent. Argument A7 demands of the patient the credentials of the agent. It's like refusing medical care to anyone who isn't a doctor.

There's also a leap between C1 and C2. Even if animals had no rights in the strict legal sense, it doesn't follow that we may do whatever we like with them. A consequentialist ethics doesn't even need the language of rights: avoidable suffering is enough to give a moral reason against it.

Newborns, people with profound intellectual disabilities and people in a coma have no duties and can't make claims. By P1's criterion, they'd have no rights. Almost no one accepts that, which is enough to reject the premise.

text.bold: 2. The law itself works this way.

paragraph.text: Guardianship exists precisely to represent those who can't make claims. Future generations, who can't reciprocate anything or take part in any agreement, appear in constitutions and environmental treaties as owed consideration. Inability to complain has never been an obstacle to legal protection.

text.bold: 3. The "it's a matter of kind" way out is circular.

paragraph.text: Cohen answers the human cases by saying moral capacity characterizes the species, not each individual. But that means judging someone by what other members of their species have, which is exactly the point in dispute. If we applied the same reasoning to intelligence, we'd say a baby can do algebra because adult humans can. Chapter A11 deals with this in detail.

Animals cooperate, return favors and punish cheating. Vampire bats share food with those who have fed them before, in a pattern of reciprocity documented by Wilkinson (1984). This doesn't make reciprocity a moral criterion, and the book doesn't want to fall into that trap. It only shows that the premise describes animals poorly.

Rawls excluded animals from the domain of justice, but affirmed duties of compassion and humanity toward them. Cohen defends their use in research and still recognizes human obligations of kindness. Conclusion C2, "so we may use them as we please", isn't supported even by the argument's own authors.

text.bold: 6. The law has already begun to move.

paragraph.text: In January 2022, Ecuador's Constitutional Court ruled, in the case of the monkey Estrellita, that individual animals are subjects of rights protected by the rights of nature, and ordered the state to produce specific legislation. In the United Kingdom, the sentience law came to recognize cephalopods and decapods. None of this required animals to take on duties.

text.bold: 7. Those who receive care needn't be able to give it.

paragraph.text: Requiring that someone be capable of acting morally in order to be considered is like requiring a patient to be a doctor in order to be treated. The beneficiaries of an activity needn't be able to perform it. See

paragraph.text: (d) The strongest counter-reply: the moral community
The strongest version doesn't say animal suffering is irrelevant. It says

are a specific instrument, born of reciprocal relationships within a moral community, and that extending them to those who can't take part in that community would be a conceptual mistake. Incapable humans would be included by belonging to the kind, and because excluding them would threaten the stability of the community itself. Animals would remain protected by indirect duties of kindness.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: It makes the protection of the vulnerable contingent.

paragraph.text: If a baby is protected because it suits social stability, then in a scenario where that convenience vanished, the protection would fall with it. Moral intuition says the opposite: the baby is protected for its own sake.

text.bold: Inclusion "by kind" is the species boundary under another name.

paragraph.text: Asked why the kind matters more than the individual, the answer comes back to "because they're human", which is A10.

text.bold: The contract's own device points the other way.

paragraph.text: Mark Rowlands showed that if the veil of ignorance also covered species, the contractors would choose rules protecting all sentient beings.

text.bold: Indirect duties would already be enough to condemn the practice.

paragraph.text: If we have duties not to cause unnecessary suffering, industrial livestock farming, with confinement, mutilation and slaughter at scale, doesn't pass even that minimal filter.

It's common for the same person to say "animals have no rights" and then "but you mustn't mistreat them". The second sentence already concedes the essential point.

They could be dominated. If protection arises from the ability to demand, those who can't demand are left unprotected
This is the historical description of colonialism, and the reason we came to speak of universal human rights

There's an important truth embedded here. Animals aren't moral agents: they can't be held responsible, tried or punished, and it would be absurd to prosecute a lion for killing a gazelle. Reciprocity also explains well the historical origin of many norms, and the word "right", in the strict legal sense, involves institutions, representation and procedures that need careful design when the holder can't speak for themselves.

But none of this supports the conclusion. The asymmetry between us and them is exactly why the responsibility is ours. Only one side of this relationship can deliberate about what it does, and that side is us.
